title: Apply Responsible AI Principles and Ethics
intro: The core principles of responsible AI and how to make them enforceable; where algorithmic bias comes from and how fairness is measured and improved across protected groups; transparency, explainability and interpretability; and the systemic, environmental and societal trade-offs of deploying AI.
objectives: Explain the core responsible AI principles, their sources, and how to turn them into requirements, controls and evidence
Identify sources of algorithmic bias, apply fairness metrics such as impact ratios and equal opportunity, and choose mitigations
Distinguish transparency, explainability and interpretability, and select appropriate explanation methods
Recognise legal duties to explain AI decisions and the security risks explanations create
Assess systemic impacts and the environmental footprint of AI, and weigh societal trade-offs responsibly

scenes.title: From principles to practice
scenes.sub: The values behind responsible AI, and how to make them enforceable
scenes.say: Almost every organisation that uses AI has published principles. Far fewer can show how those principles change what their systems actually do. | This video covers the core responsible AI principles, where they come from, and how to turn them into requirements, controls and evidence.

scenes.title: Six core principles

items.d: Treat people equitably; avoid unjust discrimination
Perform as intended and fail safely
Protect personal data and resist attack
Work for people of all abilities and backgrounds
Be open about AI use, purpose and limits
People remain answerable for AI outcomes

scenes.say: Six principles appear in almost every responsible AI framework. | Fairness: AI should treat people equitably and avoid unjust discrimination. | Reliability and safety: it should perform consistently as intended, and fail safely when it doesn’t. | Privacy and security: it should protect personal data and resist attack. | Inclusiveness: it should work for people of all abilities, languages and backgrounds, not just the majority. | Transparency: organisations should be open about when and how AI is used, what it is for, and its limitations. | And accountability: people, not machines, remain answerable for AI outcomes.

scenes.title: Where the principles come from

items.d: Adopted 2019, updated 2024; endorsed by dozens of governments

items.h: UNESCO Recommendation on the Ethics of AI
items.d: 2021; adopted by all 193 member states
Seven requirements that shaped the EU AI Act
Translate shared values into a specific organisation’s context

scenes.say: These principles have common roots. | The OECD AI Principles, adopted in twenty nineteen and updated in twenty twenty-four, are endorsed by dozens of governments, and underpin many national strategies. | UNESCO’s Recommendation on the Ethics of AI, from twenty twenty-one, was adopted by all one hundred and ninety-three member states. | The EU’s ethics guidelines for trustworthy AI set seven requirements, such as human agency and oversight, that later shaped the AI Act. | And companies adapt these shared values to their own context, products and risks.

scenes.title: Making a principle enforceable

nodes.label: Requirement
nodes.sub: error rates within 5 points across groups

note.text: No requirement, no control, no evidence: the principle is only a slogan.

scenes.say: A principle only matters when it changes behaviour. Take fairness. | First, turn it into a measurable requirement, for example: error rates for different demographic groups must stay within five percentage points of each other. | Then attach a control: a bias test before every release, and monitoring in production. | And keep evidence: test reports, monitoring dashboards and a documented sign-off. Without that chain, a principle is only a slogan.

scenes.title: Why principles fail

items.d: “Be fair” means nothing until someone defines it
Everyone agrees; nobody is accountable
Nothing is measured, so nothing improves
Concerns can be raised but never block a launch

scenes.say: Principles fail in predictable ways, a pattern sometimes called ethics washing. | Vague language: be fair means nothing until someone defines fair for this use case. | No owner: everyone agrees with the principles, and nobody is accountable for them. | No metrics: nothing is measured, so nothing improves. | And no authority to stop: concerns can be raised, but they never actually block a launch.

scenes.title: When principles collide

items.d: Explaining a fraud model can teach fraudsters to evade it
Measuring bias needs data on sensitive traits
Fairness constraints can reduce overall accuracy
Over-cautious refusals push users to riskier tools

scenes.say: Principles also conflict, and governance exists to resolve the conflicts deliberately. | Transparency and security: explaining exactly how a fraud model works can teach fraudsters to evade it. | Fairness and privacy: you can’t measure bias against a group without some data about who is in it. | Fairness and accuracy: constraining a model to equalise outcomes can reduce its overall accuracy. | And safety and helpfulness: a system that refuses too much pushes people towards less safe alternatives. The answer is a documented decision, made by people with the authority to make it.

items: Fairness, reliability and safety, privacy and security, inclusiveness, transparency, accountability
Shared roots: OECD, UNESCO, EU trustworthy AI
Principle → requirement → control → evidence
Resolve conflicts deliberately and document them
scenes.say: To recap. | The six core principles are fairness, reliability and safety, privacy and security, inclusiveness, transparency and accountability. | They share roots in the OECD, UNESCO and EU frameworks. | They only work when each principle becomes a requirement, a control and evidence. | And when principles collide, resolve the conflict deliberately, and write the decision down.

blocks.md:
### The principles in detail
| Principle | What it means in practice | Typical controls |
|---|---|---|
| **Fairness** | Similar people are treated similarly; outcomes don’t unjustly disadvantage protected groups | Bias testing across groups, representative data, fairness metrics with thresholds, monitoring |
| **Reliability and safety** | The system performs as intended across expected conditions and fails safely outside them | Evaluation against requirements, stress and adversarial testing, fallbacks, human oversight |
| **Privacy and security** | Personal data is lawfully processed and protected; the system resists attack | DPIAs, minimisation, privacy-enhancing technologies, threat modelling, security testing |
| **Inclusiveness** | The system works for people with different abilities, languages, cultures and circumstances | Accessibility testing, diverse user research, multilingual evaluation, alternative channels |
| **Transparency** | People know when AI is used, what it does, its limits, and how to challenge it | Disclosure notices, model and system cards, documentation, explanations |
| **Accountability** | Named people answer for outcomes; there are routes to redress | Ownership, governance committees, audit trails, complaint and appeal processes |

These six follow a widely used corporate formulation, and closely match the international frameworks:

- **OECD AI Principles** (2019, updated 2024): inclusive growth, sustainable development and well-being; respect for human rights and democratic values, including fairness and privacy; transparency and explainability; robustness, security and safety; and accountability.
- **UNESCO Recommendation on the Ethics of AI** (2021): ten principles, including proportionality and do no harm, safety and security, privacy, human oversight and determination, transparency and explainability, responsibility and accountability, fairness and non-discrimination, and sustainability.
- **EU High-Level Expert Group’s Ethics Guidelines for Trustworthy AI** (2019): seven requirements: human agency and oversight; technical robustness and safety; privacy and data governance; transparency; diversity, non-discrimination and fairness; societal and environmental well-being; and accountability.

### Operationalising principles
A responsible AI programme makes each principle real through the governance machinery from Module 2.1:

1. **Policy** commits the organisation to the principles.
2. **Standards** turn each principle into measurable requirements per risk tier (for example, “Tier 3 systems must report false positive rates by group and stay within agreed thresholds”).
3. **Assessments** (impact assessments, DPIAs, bias evaluations) check each use case against the requirements before approval.
4. **Controls** are built into the lifecycle: data checks, testing gates, human oversight, monitoring.
5. **Evidence** is retained: test results, sign-offs, monitoring reports, decisions on trade-offs.
6. **Escalation and authority:** a person or body (for example, the AI governance committee or an ethics officer) can delay or stop deployment when requirements aren’t met.

### Ethics washing
**Ethics washing** is presenting an appearance of ethical AI without the substance: published principles with no owners, metrics, enforcement or effect on decisions. Warning signs include principles that never block a project, ethics boards with no authority or that are disbanded when inconvenient, and transparency reports with no measurable content. Auditors and regulators increasingly look for **evidence of operation**, not statements of intent.

### Resolving conflicts between principles
Trade-offs are normal. Good practice is to:
- make the conflict explicit in the impact assessment;
- consider alternatives that reduce the conflict (for example, privacy-preserving methods for bias measurement, or explaining a fraud decision to the customer in general terms without exposing model features);
- have the decision made at the right level of authority;
- document the rationale and revisit it when circumstances change.

blocks.title: Match the control to the principle it mainly serves
pairs: Telling users they are chatting with an AI
Testing a speech assistant with diverse accents and speech impairments
Comparing false positive rates across demographic groups
Naming a business owner and an appeals process for decisions

blocks.title: Principles with teeth
blocks.md: Organisations with mature programmes can point to launches that were **delayed, changed or cancelled** because they failed a responsible AI requirement. If no project has ever been affected, the principles probably aren’t operating.

q.q: A company’s published AI principles commit it to fairness, but no fairness metric, test or owner exists for any AI system. What does this BEST illustrate?
o: Mature responsible AI governance, because the principles have been published
Ethics washing: principles without operational requirements, controls or accountability
A privacy-enhancing approach that avoids collecting data needed to measure fairness
An appropriate approach for high-risk systems, where metrics are set only after deployment
q.why: Principles only have effect when translated into measurable requirements, controls, evidence and owners. Without them, the organisation projects responsibility without practising it.

sections.title: Algorithmic bias and fairness across protected groups

scenes.title: Bias in, bias out
scenes.sub: Where algorithmic bias comes from, how to measure it, and how to reduce it
scenes.say: AI systems learn from the past, and the past is not fair. Without deliberate effort, models reproduce and even amplify historical discrimination. | This video explains where bias enters, how fairness is measured, and what you can do about it.

scenes.title: Where bias enters
scenes.say: Bias can enter at every stage. It starts with historical bias: the world that generated the data was unequal, so even perfectly collected data encodes that inequality. | Representation bias occurs when some groups are under-sampled, so the model learns less about them. | Measurement bias comes from skewed labels or proxies. Using arrests as a proxy for crime, or postcode as a proxy for creditworthiness, imports existing disparities. | Learning, or aggregation, bias appears when a single model optimised for overall accuracy fits the majority and fails smaller groups. | Evaluation bias hides the problem when test data doesn’t represent everyone the system will serve. | And deployment bias arises when a system is used beyond its intended context, or when its outputs feed back into the next round of training data.

num.label: false positive rates, Black vs white defendants (2016)

scenes.def: A widely used recidivism tool had similar overall accuracy for both groups, but its errors fell very differently.
scenes.ex: People wrongly labelled “high risk” face harsher outcomes. Equal accuracy did not mean equal treatment.
scenes.say: A famous example. In twenty sixteen, journalists analysed a recidivism risk tool used in US courts. They found that Black defendants who did not reoffend were wrongly labelled high risk about forty-five per cent of the time, against about twenty-four per cent for white defendants. | The tool’s overall accuracy was similar for both groups. Its errors were not. | People wrongly labelled high risk can face harsher bail and sentencing decisions, so equal accuracy did not mean equal treatment.

scenes.title: Four ways to define fairness

items.d: Each group is selected at the same rate
Qualified people in every group are selected at the same rate (equal TPR)
Equal true positive and false positive rates across groups
A positive prediction is equally reliable for every group (equal precision)

scenes.say: Fairness can be measured in several ways, and they don’t agree. | Demographic parity asks whether each group is selected at the same rate, regardless of other factors. | Equal opportunity asks whether qualified people in every group are selected at the same rate. In other words, equal true positive rates. | Equalised odds is stricter: equal true positive rates and equal false positive rates. | And predictive parity asks whether a positive prediction is equally reliable for every group, which means equal precision. When base rates differ between groups, it is mathematically impossible to satisfy all of these at once, so choosing the right measure is a policy decision, not a technical one.

scenes.title: The four-fifths rule

notes.d: Each group’s selection rate divided by the highest group’s rate.
Below 0.8, a common red flag for adverse impact that needs investigation.

scenes.say: A simple screening test is the four-fifths rule, from US employment guidance. Divide each group’s selection rate by the rate of the most-selected group. This is the impact ratio. | Here, group B’s rate is forty-two per cent, against sixty per cent for group A, an impact ratio of point seven. Anything below point eight is a common red flag for adverse impact. It doesn’t prove discrimination, but it demands investigation, and similar ratios appear in mandated bias audits of hiring tools.

scenes.title: Reducing bias

items.d: Better and more representative data; reweighting; remove proxy features
Fairness constraints or penalties in the learning objective
Adjust thresholds or calibrate outputs, where lawful
Diverse teams, impact assessment, human review, monitoring

scenes.say: Mitigation can happen at several points. | Before training: collect better, more representative data, reweight under-represented groups, and remove features that act as proxies for protected characteristics. | During training: add fairness constraints or penalties to the learning objective. | After training: adjust decision thresholds or calibrate outputs, where the law allows it. | And around the model: diverse teams, impact assessments, meaningful human review, and monitoring of fairness metrics in production, because bias can drift too.

items: Bias enters at every stage, starting with history
Equal accuracy can hide unequal errors
Fairness metrics conflict; choosing one is a policy decision
Mitigate before, during and after training, and monitor
scenes.say: To recap. | Bias can enter at every stage, starting with historical inequality in the data. | Equal overall accuracy can hide very unequal errors between groups. | Fairness metrics conflict, so choosing one is a policy decision that needs the right owner. | And mitigation happens before, during and after training, with monitoring in production.

blocks.md:
### Protected groups and discrimination
Most jurisdictions prohibit discrimination on the basis of **protected characteristics**. The lists vary: the UK Equality Act 2010, for example, names nine (age, disability, gender reassignment, marriage and civil partnership, pregnancy and maternity, race, religion or belief, sex, and sexual orientation), while US federal law protects characteristics such as race, colour, religion, sex, national origin, age and disability. Two forms of discrimination matter for AI:

- **Direct discrimination** (disparate treatment): treating someone less favourably *because of* a protected characteristic. A model that uses gender as an input to reject applicants does this.
- **Indirect discrimination** (disparate impact): an apparently neutral rule or model that disproportionately disadvantages a protected group without adequate justification. Most AI bias is of this kind, often through **proxies**: postcode for ethnicity, career gaps for sex, name for national origin.

Removing protected attributes from the inputs (“fairness through unawareness”) rarely works, because proxies carry the same information. In one widely reported case, an experimental recruiting model learned to downgrade CVs containing the word “women’s” (as in “women’s chess club captain”), because it had been trained on a decade of applications dominated by men. The project was abandoned.

### Sources of bias
| Source | Description | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Historical | Data reflects past inequality | Lending data shaped by past discriminatory practices |
| Representation (sampling) | Groups are under- or over-represented | Face datasets dominated by lighter-skinned faces |
| Measurement | Labels or features are flawed proxies | Healthcare cost used as a proxy for health need |
| Aggregation (learning) | One model for groups that behave differently | A diagnostic model tuned on the majority population |
| Evaluation | Benchmarks don’t reflect the deployment population | Testing speech recognition only on native speakers |
| Deployment | Use outside intended context; feedback loops | Predictive policing sending more patrols, finding more crime, reinforcing itself |

Generative AI adds **representational harms**: stereotyped images, biased associations in text, and uneven quality across languages and dialects. These are evaluated with targeted prompts and benchmarks across groups, not just with classification metrics.

### Measuring fairness
Using the confusion matrix from Module 1.3, computed **separately for each group**:

| Metric | Equal across groups | When it fits |
|---|---|---|
| **Demographic (statistical) parity** | Selection rate | When the goal is equal representation in outcomes |
| **Equal opportunity** | True positive rate (recall) | When missing qualified people is the main harm |
| **Equalised odds** | True positive and false positive rates | When both missed opportunities and wrongful flags harm people |
| **Predictive parity** | Precision | When a positive decision must mean the same for everyone |
| **Calibration within groups** | Predicted probabilities match outcomes | When scores are used directly as probabilities |

Research by Kleinberg and colleagues and by Chouldechova showed that when base rates differ between groups, a classifier generally cannot be calibrated *and* have equal false positive and false negative rates at the same time. The recidivism controversy was exactly this conflict: the vendor pointed to equal predictive parity, critics to unequal false positive rates. **Choosing the metric is a governance decision** that depends on context, law and which errors cause the most harm.

### Regulation and audits
- The **four-fifths (80%) rule** from the US Uniform Guidelines on Employee Selection Procedures treats an impact ratio below 0.8 as evidence of potential adverse impact.
- **New York City Local Law 144** requires annual independent bias audits of automated employment decision tools, with published impact ratios.
- The **EU AI Act** (Article 10) requires providers of high-risk systems to examine training, validation and test data for possible biases and take measures to detect, prevent and mitigate them. Recognising that you can’t measure bias without data about groups, the Act permits strictly necessary processing of special-category data for bias detection, with safeguards, and the 2026 Omnibus extended this permission beyond high-risk systems.

### Mitigation and monitoring
- **Pre-processing:** collect more representative data; reweight or resample; remove or transform proxy features; fix label quality.
- **In-processing:** add fairness constraints or regularisation to training; adversarial debiasing.
- **Post-processing:** adjust thresholds per group or recalibrate scores. Group-specific thresholds may be unlawful in some contexts (for example, some employment decisions), so legal advice is essential.
- **Organisational:** diverse development and review teams; stakeholder consultation with affected groups; impact assessments; human review of adverse decisions; complaint and appeal channels.
- **Monitoring:** fairness can drift as populations change. Track group metrics in production, with thresholds and owners, just like accuracy.

blocks.title: Run a fairness check
items: Define the decision and the harm
A model shortlists applicants for interview. The main harm is qualified people being wrongly rejected.
Choose metrics with the owner
The business owner, HR, legal and the ethics officer agree to track impact ratios and equal opportunity (true positive rate by group).
Get group data lawfully
Use voluntarily provided diversity data under strict access controls, or a validated proxy method approved by legal and privacy teams.
Compute and compare
Selection rates: A 60%, B 42%, C 55%, D 51%. Impact ratio for B is 0.70, below the 0.8 threshold. True positive rate for B is also lowest.
Investigate causes
Analysis shows a feature measuring continuous employment penalises career breaks, which are more common in group B.
Mitigate and re-test
Remove the feature, retrain, and re-test: B’s impact ratio rises to 0.86 with little loss of accuracy. Document the decision and add monitoring.

blocks.title: Fairness traps
blocks.md:
- **Removing the protected attribute** is not enough: proxies leak it back in.
- **Equal overall accuracy** does not mean fair: compare error rates *by group*.
- **No single metric** is universally right. When base rates differ, metrics conflict, so the choice must be justified and owned.
- **Bias is not only a data-science problem**: governance, diverse teams, impact assessment and monitoring are part of the answer.

q.q: A loan model excludes race as an input, yet approval rates differ sharply by race. Investigation finds it relies heavily on postcode. What is the MOST likely explanation?
o: The model is fair, because race isn’t one of its inputs and postcode is a neutral feature
Postcode is acting as a proxy for race, producing indirect discrimination
The model is overfitted to the training data, so its outcomes differ between areas
The disparity is most likely due to random chance in the applicant sample
q.why: Removing a protected attribute doesn’t remove its influence when correlated features act as proxies. Residential patterns make postcode a strong proxy for race in many places.

scenes.sub: Transparency, explainability and interpretability, and their limits
scenes.say: When an AI system affects someone, they reasonably ask: why? And regulators, auditors and your own staff ask the same question. | This video separates transparency, explainability and interpretability, shows how explanations are produced, and explains when explanations themselves create risk.

scenes.title: Three related ideas
rows: Is AI used, and how was it built?
A chatbot notice; a model card
Top reasons a loan was declined
scenes.say: These three terms are related but different. | Transparency answers: is AI being used, and how was it built and tested? Explainability answers: why did it produce this particular output? Interpretability answers: how does the model work inside? | A chatbot notice or a model card is transparency. The main reasons a loan was declined is an explanation. Reading the rules of a decision tree is interpretability. | And the audiences differ: transparency serves users, the public and regulators; explanations serve affected people and reviewers; interpretability serves developers, validators and auditors.

scenes.say: Here is a local explanation for one decision. Every applicant starts from the same base score, and each feature pushes the score up or down. | Two missed payments in the last year push hardest towards a decline, followed by a high debt-to-income ratio and a short credit history. | Income and years at the same address push the other way, but only a little. | The final score is point three one, below the approval threshold of point five, so the application is declined. Methods such as SHAP calculate contributions like these. | A counterfactual explanation is often more useful to the applicant: it says what would have to change for a different outcome.

scenes.title: Explaining generative AI

items.d: Show the passages an answer was grounded in
Model and system cards: purpose, data, tests, limits
A model’s stated reasoning may not reflect how it decided
Methods that inspect internal features are maturing, not yet routine

scenes.say: Large generative models are much harder to explain. | The most practical explanation is provenance: show the passages an answer was grounded in, so people can check them. | Document the system with model and system cards, covering purpose, training data, evaluations and known limitations. | Treat a model’s own explanation of its reasoning with caution. Research shows that stated reasoning doesn’t always reflect how the model actually reached its answer. | And interpretability research, which inspects the internal features of a model, is advancing quickly, but it is not yet a routine assurance tool.

scenes.title: Rights to transparency and explanation

items.d: Meaningful information about the logic of automated decisions
Human intervention and the right to contest
Providers must give deployers clear instructions and limits
Disclose AI interaction; explain high-risk decisions

scenes.say: Explanations are increasingly a legal duty. | Under the GDPR, people must receive meaningful information about the logic involved in automated decisions about them. | Article twenty-two adds the right to human intervention and to contest solely automated decisions with significant effects. | Under the AI Act, providers of high-risk systems must give deployers clear instructions, including capabilities, limitations and how to interpret outputs. | And people must be told when they interact with AI, while those affected by decisions based on certain high-risk systems gain a right to a clear and meaningful explanation.

scenes.title: When explanations create risk

items.d: Detailed explanations help attackers copy or game the model
Explanations can reveal information about training data
Plausible reasons that don’t match how the model decided
Tailor explanations to each audience

scenes.say: Explanations also carry risk. | Detailed, per-feature explanations can help attackers reconstruct a model, or learn exactly how to evade it. | Explanations can leak information about the training data, which is a privacy risk. | Post-hoc explanations can be plausible but unfaithful, describing reasons that don’t match how the model really decided. | And too much detail confuses people. Give affected individuals clear reasons and recourse, give reviewers more depth, and reserve full technical detail for validators and auditors.

items: Transparency: that AI is used; explainability: why; interpretability: how
Local explanations and counterfactuals help affected people
Generative AI: cite sources; distrust self-explanations
Explanations are rights, and can also leak and mislead

blocks.md:
### Definitions
- **Transparency** is openness about an AI system: that it exists and is being used, its purpose, how it was developed, what data it uses, how it was tested, and its limitations. It operates at the level of the system and organisation.
- **Explainability** is the ability to give a human-understandable reason for a particular output or decision (a *local* explanation) or for the model’s general behaviour (a *global* explanation).
- **Interpretability** is the degree to which a human can understand the model’s internal mechanics: how inputs are transformed into outputs.

A linear model or a short decision tree is **intrinsically interpretable**. A deep neural network or large language model is not, so we rely on **post-hoc** methods that approximate or probe its behaviour.

### Common explanation methods
| Method | Type | What it gives |
|---|---|---|
| Intrinsically interpretable models (linear models, decision trees, rule lists, generalised additive models) | Global and local | The model *is* the explanation |
| Permutation feature importance | Global | Which features matter most overall |
| **SHAP** (Shapley additive explanations) | Local and global | Each feature’s contribution to a specific prediction, based on game theory |
| **LIME** (local interpretable model-agnostic explanations) | Local | A simple surrogate model that mimics the complex model near one input |
| **Counterfactual explanations** | Local | The smallest change to the inputs that would change the outcome |
| Saliency and attention maps | Local | Which pixels or tokens influenced an output (use with caution) |
| Model cards, system cards, datasheets for datasets | Transparency | Purpose, data, evaluation results, limitations and intended use |

**Counterfactuals** are often the most useful for affected people because they are actionable (“if your outstanding debt were £2,000 lower, you would have been approved”) and reveal little about the model’s internals.

The supposed **accuracy–interpretability trade-off** is real for some tasks, such as image and language understanding, but for many tabular decision problems, well-designed interpretable models perform almost as well as black boxes. For high-stakes decisions, consider whether an interpretable model is good enough before choosing an opaque one.

### Explaining generative AI
- **Grounding and citations** let people verify answers against sources.
- **System and model cards** document intended use, evaluations, safety testing and known limitations.
- **Self-explanations are unreliable.** A model’s chain-of-thought or explanation of its own reasoning is generated text and may not faithfully reflect the computation that produced the answer.
- **Mechanistic interpretability**, which identifies internal features and circuits, is an active research area with promising results, but it is not yet a standard assurance technique.

### Legal duties
- **GDPR** Articles 13–15 require meaningful information about the logic involved in automated decision-making, and its significance and envisaged consequences. Article 22 gives rights to human intervention, to express a view and to contest solely automated decisions with significant effects.
- **EU AI Act** Article 13 requires high-risk systems to be transparent enough for deployers to interpret outputs and use them appropriately, with instructions covering capabilities, limitations and accuracy. Article 50 requires disclosure of AI interaction and labelling of synthetic content. Article 86 gives people affected by decisions based on high-risk systems (listed in Annex III) the right to clear and meaningful explanations of the AI’s role and the main elements of the decision.

### Security and privacy considerations
Explanations are an information channel. Rich, per-query feature attributions can help adversaries **extract** a model or craft inputs that **evade** it, and can leak details of training data. Balance this by tailoring depth to the audience, rate-limiting explanation interfaces, and providing counterfactual or reason-code explanations to the public while reserving detailed attributions for authorised reviewers.

blocks.title: Explainability vocabulary
cards: Why the model produced one particular output.
What drives the model’s behaviour overall.
A method that assigns each feature a contribution to a prediction, based on Shapley values from game theory.
A method that fits a simple surrogate model around one input to approximate the complex model locally.
The smallest change to the inputs that would have changed the outcome.
A short document describing a model’s purpose, data, performance across groups, and limitations.

blocks.title: The detailed explanation API
blocks.md: A bank exposes a public API that returns a credit score plus SHAP contributions for every feature, for unlimited queries. A security review notices automated clients submitting thousands of slightly varied applications.

q.q: What is the MOST appropriate response?
o: Remove all explanations from the API, since they are optional and create a data leakage risk
Give applicants reason codes and counterfactuals, limit detailed attributions to reviewers, and monitor the API
Return more features in each explanation, so applicants receive the most complete account possible
Keep the current API unchanged, because explanations are a legal requirement that can’t be restricted
q.why: Unlimited, detailed attributions enable model extraction and evasion. Tailoring explanations by audience, while still meeting legal duties to applicants, and adding rate limits and monitoring balances transparency with security.

q.q: An applicant asks why they were refused and what they could do differently. Which type of explanation BEST serves them?
o: A copy of the model’s full source code and its configuration files
A counterfactual explanation describing what changes would lead to approval
A global feature-importance chart showing what matters across all customers
The model’s training loss curve and its overall accuracy on the test set
q.why: Counterfactuals are local, understandable and actionable, and reveal relatively little about the model’s internals. The other options are either irrelevant to the individual or expose unnecessary detail.

sections.title: Systemic impacts, sustainability and societal trade-offs

scenes.title: Beyond the single system
scenes.sub: Systemic impacts, environmental costs and the trade-offs behind every deployment
scenes.say: Most risk assessments look at one system at a time. But AI also changes labour markets, information ecosystems, energy demand and who holds power. | This video covers those systemic impacts, the environmental footprint of AI, and how to weigh societal trade-offs responsibly.

scenes.title: Systemic impacts

items.d: Tasks automated; roles changed; skills eroded
Cheap, convincing misinformation at scale
Dependence on a few model and cloud providers
Many organisations sharing one model share its failures
Energy, water and hardware at growing scale
Surveillance, exclusion and erosion of trust

scenes.say: Systemic impacts emerge when AI is used widely, not just in one place. | Work and skills: tasks are automated, roles change, and skills people no longer practise can fade. | Information integrity: generative AI makes convincing misinformation cheap to produce at scale. | Concentration: much of the economy now depends on a handful of model and cloud providers. | Monoculture: when many organisations build on the same model, they share its vulnerabilities and failures, so one flaw can hit thousands of systems at once. | Environment: AI’s energy, water and hardware demands are growing quickly. | And rights and trust: surveillance, exclusion of people the systems serve poorly, and an erosion of trust in what we see and hear.

num.label: projected data centre electricity use in 2030 (IEA)

scenes.def: Data centres used about 415 TWh in 2024, around 1.5% of global electricity. AI is the main driver of growth.
scenes.ex: Inference often outweighs training over a model’s life, because it runs billions of times.
scenes.say: Here is the scale of the environmental question. The International Energy Agency projects that data centres will use around nine hundred and forty-five terawatt hours of electricity by twenty thirty. | That is more than double the roughly four hundred and fifteen terawatt hours they used in twenty twenty-four, about one and a half per cent of global electricity, with AI the main driver of growth. | And while training a frontier model is energy-intensive, inference, the everyday use of models, often outweighs it over a model’s lifetime, because it runs billions of times.

scenes.title: Reducing AI’s footprint

items.d: Use the smallest model that meets the requirement
Quantisation, distillation, caching and batching
Low-carbon regions and times for flexible workloads
Energy, carbon and water per system and per use

scenes.say: Sustainability is now part of responsible AI, and many measures also cut cost. | Right-size the model: use the smallest model that meets the requirement, rather than the largest available. | Make inference efficient with quantisation, distillation into smaller models, caching repeated answers, and batching requests. | Choose where and when: run flexible workloads, such as training and batch jobs, in regions and at times with low-carbon electricity. | And measure and report energy, carbon and water use per system, so decisions are based on data. Providers of general-purpose models under the EU AI Act must document known or estimated energy consumption.

scenes.title: Trade-offs you will have to make

items.d: The most accurate model may be the hardest to explain
Stronger privacy protection can reduce accuracy
Bigger models cost more energy and money
Faster launch means less testing and oversight

scenes.say: Every deployment involves trade-offs. | Accuracy and explainability: the most accurate model may be the hardest to explain. | Privacy and utility: techniques that protect privacy, such as adding noise, can reduce accuracy. | Capability and footprint: larger models cost more energy, water and money. | And speed and assurance: launching faster means less time for testing, impact assessment and oversight.

scenes.intro: A structured, repeatable way to weigh benefits and harms.

stages.label: Identify stakeholders
stages.d: Including people affected but not using the system.

stages.label: Weigh benefits and harms
stages.d: And who receives each: are they shared fairly?

stages.label: Consider alternatives

scenes.say: A structured approach helps. | First, identify stakeholders, including people affected by the system who never use it, such as job applicants or the public. | Then weigh the benefits against the harms, and ask who receives each. A system that benefits the organisation while shifting the risk onto vulnerable people needs strong justification. | Consider alternatives, including a non-AI solution, or not proceeding at all. | Make the decision at the right level of authority, record the reasons, and then monitor and revisit it as use grows and impacts change.

scenes.say: To recap. | AI has systemic impacts on work, information integrity, market concentration and the shared failure modes of monoculture. | Its environmental footprint is growing fast, with data centre electricity use projected to more than double by twenty thirty. | Right-size models, make inference efficient, and measure energy and carbon. | And weigh not just total benefits and harms, but who benefits and who bears the risk, and document why you decided.

blocks.md:
### Systemic impacts
A **systemic impact** arises from the widespread or interconnected use of AI, rather than from one system. Individual risk assessments often miss them, so governance needs to look up from the single use case.

- **Labour and skills.** AI automates tasks more often than entire jobs, but changes can be rapid and uneven. Deskilling is a subtle risk: if analysts rely on AI triage for years, their ability to investigate without it may fade, which matters when the AI fails. Responsible deployment includes reskilling, consultation with workers and, in many jurisdictions, legal duties to inform or consult employee representatives.
- **Information integrity.** Generative AI lowers the cost of persuasive misinformation, impersonation and fraud. Deepfake voice scams against businesses and synthetic disinformation around elections are documented risks. Content provenance and labelling (Module 2.6) are part of the response.
- **Concentration and dependency.** A small number of companies supply frontier models, cloud capacity and accelerators. This concentrates economic power and creates **single points of failure**: a provider outage, price change, policy change or compromise can affect thousands of organisations at once.
- **Monoculture and correlated failure.** When many organisations build on the same foundation model, a jailbreak technique, vulnerability or bias in that model is shared by all of them. From a security perspective, this is a supply-chain concentration risk (Module 2.5).
- **Homogenisation.** Widespread use of the same models can narrow the diversity of content and decisions, a risk named in the NIST Generative AI Profile.
- **Rights and inclusion.** Surveillance, profiling and systems that work poorly for some groups can exclude people from services or chill free expression.

The EU AI Act addresses one category explicitly: **general-purpose AI models with systemic risk**, whose providers must assess and mitigate risks at Union level, perform adversarial testing, track and report serious incidents, and ensure cybersecurity.

### Sustainability
AI’s environmental footprint has three main parts:

| Component | Driver | Mitigations |
|---|---|---|
| **Energy and carbon** | Training and, increasingly, inference at scale; carbon intensity of the grid | Smaller and efficient models; quantisation and distillation; caching; carbon-aware scheduling; renewable energy procurement |
| **Water** | Cooling data centres, directly and through power generation | Efficient cooling designs; siting decisions; measuring water usage effectiveness (WUE) |
| **Hardware** | Manufacturing accelerators and servers; short refresh cycles; e-waste | Longer hardware life; utilisation monitoring; responsible disposal and recycling |

The International Energy Agency estimated that data centres used about **415 TWh in 2024 (around 1.5% of global electricity)** and projected this would more than double to around **945 TWh by 2030**, driven largely by AI. Useful efficiency metrics include **power usage effectiveness (PUE)**, energy per inference, and carbon per thousand requests. Sustainability reporting regimes, such as the EU Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive, increasingly require organisations to disclose material environmental impacts, and providers of general-purpose AI models must document known or estimated energy consumption.

### Societal trade-offs
Responsible AI does not mean zero risk; it means **deliberate, accountable choices**. A sound trade-off analysis:
1. Identifies all stakeholders, including those affected but not consulted by default.
2. Assesses benefits and harms, and their **distribution**: who gains, who bears the risk, and whether vulnerable groups carry a disproportionate share.
3. Considers alternatives, including non-AI approaches and the option not to proceed (“just because we can doesn’t mean we should”).
4. Is decided at the appropriate level, with the rationale documented in the impact assessment.
5. Is monitored and revisited, because impacts change with scale.

blocks.title: Trade-off case studies
items: Call-centre automation

**Benefit:** faster service, lower cost. **Harm:** job losses; worse service for people who struggle with automated channels. **Balanced decision:** automate routine requests, keep an easy route to a human, retrain staff for complex cases, and monitor complaint rates by customer group.
Public-sector fraud detection

**Benefit:** reduced fraud. **Harm:** false accusations against vulnerable claimants, which have caused serious public scandals in several countries. **Balanced decision:** human review before any adverse action, published criteria, fairness testing, and accessible appeals.
Frontier model for internal search

**Benefit:** best answer quality. **Harm:** high cost and energy use for a task a smaller model handles well. **Balanced decision:** evaluate smaller models first; route only complex queries to the large model.
Facial recognition for building access

**Benefit:** convenience. **Harm:** biometric privacy risks, accuracy differences across groups, and function creep. **Balanced decision:** offer a non-biometric alternative, test accuracy across groups, conduct a DPIA, and strictly limit purpose and retention.

blocks.title: Systemic risk from a security angle
blocks.md: If many business units, or many organisations, rely on the **same model or provider**, a single vulnerability, outage or policy change becomes a **correlated, systemic failure**. Mitigations include provider diversity for critical services, tested fallbacks, contractual protections, and tracking model dependencies in the inventory and AIBOM.

q.q: Several critical business processes all depend on one externally hosted foundation model. Which risk does this MOST directly create?
o: Model collapse, as the shared model is retrained on its own outputs
Concentration risk: one provider outage, change or flaw could disrupt them all at once
Data drift, because each business process sends the shared model very different kinds of data
Aleatoric uncertainty, because the provider’s model is non-deterministic
q.why: Heavy dependence on one model or provider creates a single point of failure and correlated risk. Fallbacks, provider diversity and contractual protections reduce it.

quiz.q: Which principle is MOST directly served by telling users they are interacting with an AI system?
o: Fairness
Transparency
Reliability
Inclusiveness
quiz.why: Disclosing AI use is a core transparency measure, and a legal duty under Article 50 of the EU AI Act for systems that interact with people.

o: Removing personal data from training sets before a model is published or shared
Projecting ethical AI through published principles without requirements, controls or accountability
Retraining a model on rebalanced data to reduce bias before an external audit
Commissioning an independent audit of AI ethics and publishing a short summary of its findings on the website
quiz.why: Ethics washing is the appearance of responsible AI without substance: principles that have no owners, metrics or effect on decisions.

quiz.q: Which principle focuses on ensuring AI works well for people of different abilities, languages and backgrounds?
o: Accountability
Inclusiveness
Privacy
Security
quiz.why: Inclusiveness means designing and testing for diverse users, including people with disabilities and speakers of different languages and dialects.

quiz.q: A hiring tool shortlists 30% of female applicants and 50% of male applicants. What is the impact ratio, and what does it suggest under the four-fifths rule?
o: 1.67; no concern, because women are shortlisted more efficiently
0.6; potential adverse impact requiring investigation
0.8; exactly at the threshold, so there is no concern
0.2; proof that the tool discriminates intentionally
quiz.why: Impact ratio = 30 ÷ 50 = 0.6, below 0.8, which is a common indicator of potential adverse impact. It requires investigation but is not, on its own, proof of discrimination.

quiz.q: Which fairness metric requires equal true positive rates across groups?
o: Demographic parity
Equal opportunity
Predictive parity
Calibration
quiz.why: Equal opportunity requires that qualified (actually positive) people in each group are correctly selected at the same rate.

quiz.q: Why does removing protected attributes from a model’s inputs often fail to prevent discrimination?
o: Models give little weight to demographic inputs, so removing them changes nothing
Other features, such as postcode, act as proxies carrying the same information
Protected attributes are legally required inputs in every high-risk model
Removing inputs makes the model so accurate that small groups are overlooked
quiz.why: Features such as postcode, name or career gaps can correlate strongly with protected characteristics and reproduce the same disparities.

quiz.q: What does a counterfactual explanation describe?
o: The model’s full architecture, including its layers and the weights that matter most
The smallest change to the inputs that would have produced a different outcome
The average importance of each feature across all of the model’s predictions
The training data used to build the model and how each record influenced it
quiz.why: Counterfactuals are local and actionable: “if X had been different, the decision would have been Y”.

quiz.q: How does transparency differ from explainability?
o: They mean the same thing: both describe publishing a model’s source code and weights
Transparency is openness about a system’s use, design and limits; explainability gives reasons for outputs
Transparency applies only to open-source code, while explainability applies to every AI system
Explainability applies only to simple linear models, while transparency applies to deep learning models as well
quiz.why: Transparency operates at the system and organisational level; explainability addresses why the system produced a specific output or behaves as it does.

quiz.q: Which practice MOST reduces an AI service’s energy footprint while maintaining quality?
o: Always using the largest available model, because it completes tasks in fewer attempts
Choosing the smallest model that meets requirements, with efficient inference such as quantisation and caching
Running heavy workloads at peak grid demand, when renewable energy supply is usually at its very highest level
Retraining the model every day on fresh data so that it never wastes energy on outdated answers
quiz.why: Right-sizing models and efficient inference cut energy and cost, often with little or no quality loss for the task.

quiz.q: What does “monoculture” risk mean in the context of AI?
o: A training dataset that contains text in only one language, which limits fairness for other speakers
Many organisations relying on the same model share its flaws, so one failure can cause correlated harm
A model trained for a single narrow task, which can’t adapt when the business needs change
A team that depends on a single data scientist, creating key-person risk for every AI project
quiz.why: Widespread dependence on the same foundation model concentrates risk: a single jailbreak, vulnerability or outage affects everyone built on it.

exam.q: An AI ethics board concludes that a planned customer-scoring system breaches the organisation’s fairness principle, but the product team launches anyway because the board is advisory. What is the BEST improvement?
o: Publish the fairness principle more prominently on the intranet, so that product teams can’t claim they were unaware of it
Give a designated body authority to block failing high-risk launches, or require documented executive risk acceptance
Disband the ethics board, since advice that teams can ignore has no effect on outcomes
Ask the product team to self-certify fairness for future launches, with spot checks by the board
exam.why: Principles need decision rights. Either a body with authority to stop non-compliant launches, or an explicit, documented acceptance by an accountable executive, turns ethical review into governance.

exam.q: A bank’s model has similar overall accuracy for two groups, but one group experiences far more wrongful denials. When choosing a fairness metric to monitor, what is MOST important?
o: Choosing the metric on which the model performs best, so that monitoring produces few false alarms
Choosing the metric that reflects the main harm, here unequal error rates, agreed by accountable owners
Using overall accuracy, since it is already equal across the two groups and is easy to explain
Monitoring every available fairness metric equally, so that no possible form of bias can be missed
exam.why: Fairness metrics conflict when base rates differ, so tracking every metric equally can’t settle which one matters; the choice is a governance decision tied to the harm in context. Overall accuracy hides unequal errors.

exam.q: To test a model for ethnic bias, the data science team needs ethnicity data that the organisation doesn’t normally collect. The privacy officer is concerned. What is the BEST approach?
o: Abandon bias testing, because processing sensitive data creates more risk than it removes
Infer ethnicity from customers’ names and postcodes, avoiding the need to collect new data
Process it only where lawful and strictly necessary for bias testing, with safeguards, documented in a DPIA
Collect ethnicity data from all customers and add it as a model input, so that bias can be corrected directly
exam.why: Bias can’t be measured without some group data. Laws such as the EU AI Act permit strictly necessary processing for bias detection with safeguards. Using ethnicity as an input, or uncontrolled inference, creates new harms.

exam.q: A regulator asks a lender to explain why its deep-learning model declined a particular applicant. What is the BEST response?
o: Provide the full model weights and code, so the regulator can reproduce the decision independently
A validated local explanation (reason codes or a counterfactual), with model documentation and the review record
State that deep-learning models can’t be explained, but that the model is accurate on average
Provide the model’s global accuracy and its fairness metrics, which show that it treats applicants consistently
exam.why: A faithful local explanation addresses the specific decision; documentation and the review record show how the system and oversight work. Weights are neither meaningful nor appropriate to share, and “can’t be explained” fails the duty.

exam.q: Auditors plan to rely on the step-by-step reasoning that an LLM writes in its output as evidence of how decisions were made. What is the MAIN concern?
o: Reasoning text is usually too short to show every step the model took
A model’s self-explanation may not reflect how it actually produced the output
LLMs can only produce reasoning text when they are run at a high temperature
Reasoning text belongs to the model provider, so auditors can’t rely on it as evidence
exam.why: Generated reasoning is itself model output. Stronger evidence includes logged inputs, retrieved sources, model versions, decision records and the human review trail.

exam.q: A city council plans to use AI to flag possible benefit fraud. Which approach BEST addresses the societal trade-offs?
o: Deploy quickly to a pilot area, then fix any problems as complaints arrive from affected residents and advocates
Assess who is harmed and how, weigh alternatives, require human review before action, and offer appeals and monitoring
Use the system only for claimants in deprived areas, where the council assumes fraud risk is higher
Keep the system’s existence confidential, so that claimants can’t learn how to avoid being flagged by it
exam.why: Public-sector fraud systems have caused serious harm to vulnerable people when deployed without safeguards. A structured trade-off analysis with oversight, recourse and monitoring is essential; targeting vulnerable groups would be discriminatory.
